div.p: BACKGROUND Glioblastoma (GB) typically recurs locally and maintains a glial histopathological phenotype. Sarcomatoid transformation is rare, and distal extra-axial recurrence with bone and soft tissue involvement is exceptionally uncommon. Molecular features of such sarcomatoid transformations remain poorly described.

div.head: OBSERVATIONS
div.p: The authors present the case of a 53-year-old man with a history of right temporal GB (IDH-wildtype, MGMT-unmethylated) treated with maximal safe resection and chemoradiotherapy. Eleven months postoperatively, surveillance MRI demonstrated local enhancement with a new left parasagittal extra-axial lesion with bony and subgaleal extension. Debulking and resection revealed a high-grade sarcomatoid tumor with focal glial immunophenotype, mimicking a secondary gliosarcoma but with near-complete predominance of the sarcomatous component. Molecular analysis demonstrated preservation of TERT, PIK3CA, and PTEN variants identified in the original GB, with acquisition of a TP53 mutation. LESSONS This case illustrates a rare pattern of GB progression, characterized by distal extra-axial recurrence with sarcomatoid transformation. The shared driver TERT, PIK3CA, and PTEN mutations in the original right temporal and subsequent left extra-axial lesion support clonal evolution, while the newly acquired TP53 alteration may underlie histological shift. Clinicians should consider histological transformation when evaluating atypical or extracranial recurrences, as molecular continuity with the primary tumor can guide interpretation of tumor biology and recurrence patterns.

Glioblastoma (GB) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults, with a median survival of approximately 15 months despite maximal safe resection and chemoradiotherapy. 1 Recurrence is nearly universal and, in most cases (approximately 80%), arises at or near the resection margin. 2 Distant intracranial or extracranial metastases are exceedingly rare, reported in only 0.2%-1.2% of cases. The majority of recurrent GBs retain the molecular profile of the primary tumor. 3 Gliosarcoma (GS), a rare glial-sarcomatous variant of GB comprising 1%-2% of cases, 4 may occur de novo or secondarily following treatment of GB, often after radiotherapy. [5][6][7][8] The timeline of secondary GS development is variable, but the median time to progression from first diagnosis of GB is approximately 11-14 months and from irradiation (mean 55 Gy) 44.8 weeks, and the median survival after diagnosis of secondary GS is approximately 6 months. 7,9,10 Secondary GS typically demonstrates overlapping molecular features with GB but distinct biphasic morphology. 5,6 Compared to GB, GS has a higher propensity for extra-axial, dural, and osseous spread. 10,11 Importantly, both glial and sarcomatous components of GS are thought to arise from a single clonal precursor, wherein the mutational burden and molecular profiles within the same tumor are generally preserved. 12 To our knowledge, distal extra-axial recurrence with sarcomatoid transformation, accompanied by preservation of primary driver mutations and acquisition of a TP53 alteration, has not previously been reported with detailed molecular characterization. 7,[12][13][14] We present such a case to illustrate a rare pattern of clonal gliosarcomatous evolution. absence seizures. CT of the head revealed a 3.8 × 3.5 × 5.2-cm multilocular cystic, rim-enhancing lesion in the right temporal lobe (Fig. 1A). Extensive peritumoral vasogenic edema was present, with 11 mm of midline shift to the left, right cerebral convexity sulcal effacement, and early signs of right uncal herniation. One week later he developed expressive aphasia, left facial droop, and unsteady gait. Repeat CT showed no radiographic progression, but given his neurological decline, levetiracetam was initiated for seizure prophylaxis and dexamethasone for edema. CT imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of metastatic disease. MRI with gadolinium confirmed a heterogeneously enhancing right temporal mass concerning for GB, and the patient was transferred urgently to our center within 48 hours.

He underwent right craniotomy and temporal lobectomy. Intraoperatively, the tumor demonstrated thrombosed veins and hypervascularity consistent with GB. No abnormal or noncharacteristic dural or bony involvement was noted. The procedure was tolerated without perioperative complications. Histopathological analysis revealed GB, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4, without MGMT promoter methylation (Fig. 2). Following multidisciplinary consultation, the patient received 6 weeks of concurrent chemoradiotherapy followed by 6 months of adjuvant temozolomide (TMZ) according to the Stupp protocol. Three-month follow-up CT of the head demonstrated residual disease in the resection cavity, which was later declared stable with interval decrease in October 2023.

Eleven months postoperatively, surveillance MRI redemonstrated focal enhancement at the resection cavity (Fig. 1D), consistent with local recurrence, and, notably, a separate left parasagittal extra-axial mass with dural, bony, and subgaleal extension (Fig. 1H). The lesion demonstrated leptomeningeal enhancement and was associated with significant vasogenic edema. Perfusion-weighted imaging showed elevated relative cerebral blood volume ratios up to 2.2, raising concern for neoplasm. Clinically, the patient reported rapid progression of right lower extremity weakness over a 3-week period, accompanied by falls, sleep disturbance, and significant mood lability with suicidal ideation in the context of his neurological decline.

The case was reviewed at multidisciplinary neuro-oncology rounds with the neuroradiology, neurosurgery, oncology, and pathology departments. The consensus was to obtain tissue diagnosis of the secondary lesion. Repeat staging CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis again showed no systemic malignancy. At the time of surgery, which occurred 2 weeks following radiographic evidence of recurrence, the patient continued to experience rapid neurological decline, with complete loss of right lower extremity function and visual progression of the scalp protrusion overlying the extracranial component. Resection of the subgaleal, bony, and intracranial tumor components was performed. Intraoperatively, the lesion had clear involvement of the dura mater, bone, and extracranial soft tissue, with focal thickening of the pia-arachnoid but no gross parenchymal invasion. No intraoperative complications occurred.

Postoperative CT demonstrated residual tumor involving adjacent dura with probable invasion of the superior sagittal sinus. Despite no new neurological findings postoperatively, the patient continued to rapidly decline and, following tissue diagnosis, elected to proceed without further medical intervention. He died 2 weeks later.

div.head: Pathology
div.p: The initial right temporal resection (February 2023) demonstrated a high-grade astrocytic neoplasm composed of pleomorphic GFAPpositive cells within a fibrillary stroma (Fig. 2A and B). Classic GB features were present, including pseudopalisading necrosis, microvascular thrombosis, and microvascular proliferation with endothelial hyperplasia. Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse GFAP positivity, retained ATRX nuclear expression (Fig. 2D), and absence of IDH1 R132H staining (Fig. 2C). Approximately 40% of tumor nuclei were p53-positive, consistent with TP53-wildtype status (Fig. 2E), and the Ki-67 proliferative index exceeded 20% in hotspots (Fig. 2F). Molecular profiling revealed no MGMT promoter methylation (methylation-specific semiquantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction). Next-generation sequencing (NGS; Illumina NextSeq) identified TERT promoter mutation (c.146C>T, C250T), a PIK3CA gain-of-function variant (p.Arg88Gln), and a PTEN loss-of-function variant (p.Arg233*). No mutations were detected in multiple additional genes, including IDH1/2, ATRX, TP53, H3F3A, HIST1H3B, EGFR, and BRAF, and no copy number variants were detected. Chromosomal single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) microarray analysis (Illumina Infinium) showed loss of an entire chromosome 10, but no gain of a whole chromosome 7, and neither amplification of EGFR nor deletion of CDKN2A/B was detected. The integrated diagnosis was GB, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4 (Table 1).

The recurrence (January 2024) yielded an extra-axial, dural, and intraosseous lesion composed predominantly of spindle-shaped pleomorphic cells arranged in fascicles within a dense collagen-rich stroma, conferring a sarcomatoid appearance (Fig. 3A-C and E). Some focal glioma-like immunophenotypic features were noted. However, a highgrade glioma histological pattern was not present, and consequently the tumor did not exhibit characteristic GS features, based on 2021 WHO CNS 5th Edition diagnostic criteria. Immunohistochemistry revealed diffuse vimentin positivity (Fig. 3F), focal GFAP (10%-15% of overall tumor cell population) (Fig. 3D), focal S100, and strong diffuse nuclear p53 expression (Fig. 3G). There was focal reactivity for pancytokeratin, and focal immunolabeling of some tumor cells for smooth muscle actin (SMA) and desmin, supporting mesenchymal differentiation. The Ki-67 proliferative index ranged from 15% to 20% (Fig. 3H). The bony tumor infiltrate had predominantly sarcomatoid features (Fig. 4) with focal necrosis. NGS analysis identified TERT, PIK3CA, and PTEN alterations identical to those in the primary tumor, with the addition of a TP53 loss-of-function missense mutation (p.Met237Ile) involving the DNA-binding domain of the p53 protein. 15 MGMT promoter methylation remained absent. Chromosomal SNP microarray was attempted on samples from two different areas of the tumor, but failed to yield DNA of sufficient quality for copy number analysis. No tissue selected for SNP had undergone decalcification, which may otherwise degrade DNA and interfere with availability for analysis. Regardless, we realistically anticipate that the loss of chromosome 10 detected in the primary GB would persist in the recurrent tumor, given what is known about the molecular phenotypes of both tumors. The integrated findings indicated a high-grade sarcomatoid tumor with focal glial immunophenotype, consistent with sarcomatoid transformation of GB (Table 1). CSF and serum markers were not assessed for this patient in keeping with goals of care and the short timeline between presentation and death.

div.head: Informed Consent
div.p: The necessary informed consent was obtained in this study.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Observations GS is a rare variant of GB distinguished by its mesenchymal differentiation and propensity for atypical patterns of dissemination. While it accounts for only 1%-2% of malignant gliomas, GS demonstrates a distinct biological behavior with greater metastatic potential (11%) compared with typical GB (0.2%-1.2%), particularly to dura, bone, TABLE 1. div.head: quality) Molecular evolution
div.p: Baseline profile Acquisition of TP53 mutation, otherwise identical driver mutations and extracranial sites. Secondary GS arising from a previously irradiated GB is even less common, and most transformations occur locally at the site of the original tumor. [16][17][18] In the present case, no tissue was obtained from the local recurrence within the initial right temporal resection cavity, limiting our ability to determine whether sarcomatoid transformation preceded or followed the development of the distal lesion. Additionally, while there were clear GFAP-positive cellular components within the tumor, the sarcomatoid prominence of the contralateral recurrence complicates definitive classification given the paucity of glial features. However, the preservation of the primary tumor's molecular drivers (TERT, PTEN, and PIK3CA) could suggest a shared clonal origin. The acquisition of a TP53 mutation in the recurrent tumor may further reflect a stepwise progression involving local transformation followed by distal dissemination of a newly evolved sarcomatous subclone. The prevalence of TP53 mutations in secondary GSs is nearly twice that observed in primary GBs. 19 Moreover, identical TP53 mutations have been found in both the gliomatous and sarcomatous components of GS, supporting a shared glial origin of these subpopulations. 20 Minor TP53-mutant clones within primary tumors may also contribute to treatment resistance and the outgrowth of aggressive sarcomatoid subclones. 21 Notably, mutations affecting the TP53 DNAbinding domain are associated with reduced inhibition of N-cadherin and vimentin expression and impaired suppression of cell viability in clonogenic assays, suggesting that TP53 dysfunction promotes epithelial-mesenchymal transition phenotypes. 21 Taken together with evidence that both radiation and TMZ may induce mutagenesis within the TP53 DNA-binding domain, 22 the newly acquired TP53 variant in this case may represent a treatment-resistant or treatment-derived subclonal population with enhanced mesenchymal potential and metastatic competence.

Reports of noncontiguous recurrence are exceedingly rare. One case has described a GS lesion arising at the left frontal base following a right cingulate GB tumor, although molecular profiling was not performed. 14 In a larger series of 30 patients with secondary GS, no other noncontiguous recurrences were identified, underscoring the rarity of this progression pattern. 23 Our case differs in that the patient developed a distal, extra-axial lesion with dural, bony, and subgaleal involvement, while also demonstrating molecular continuity with the primary GB and acquisition of a new genetic alteration.

The mechanism of sarcomatous transformation remains incompletely understood. Although prior reports link this process to radiotherapy, the secondary lesion in our case arose outside the radiation field. A potential model involves initial local transformation of the GB into a gliosarcomatous phenotype, followed by metastatic spread to the contralateral convexity. 7,22 This interpretation is supported by the preserved molecular profile and mutational evolution. Leptomeningeal and CSF dissemination are both described pathways in GS, which may underlie this distant progression pattern. 10,24,25 Importantly, the recurrent tumor in our case was composed almost entirely of sarcomatoid elements, with only focal glial features. This finding strongly aligns with prior literature reporting that metastatic foci of GS are often purely sarcomatous, and that the sarcoma component is the principal driver of distal and extracranial metastasis, often through hematogenous spread, whereas GB alone rarely spreads outside the CNS. [26][27][28][29] Consequently, we speculate that the local recurrence in the right temporal resection cavity was very likely a histologically conventional GS. The acquisition of a TP53 missense mutation, definitively established by NGS in the distal recurrent tumor, may have facilitated mesenchymal transition, enhanced metastatic potential, and accounted for the atypical clinical trajectory observed. 21,30,31 Alternative mechanisms in this case may include multicentricity of the primary GB, or distal GB recurrence through subventricular zone (SVZ) spread with transformation of the seeded recurrence. Multicentric GB originates from a single common clone that can spread multifocally to form distinct tumors with their own late-stage genetic mutations, either simultaneously or up to 22 years later. [32][33][34] This ancestral clone acquires a driver-mutation set (e.g., PTEN loss or TERT promoter mutations), while its migrant subclones often generate heterogeneous profiles including differences in TP53 or EGFR mutations between foci. 35,36 A case of a multicentric multifocal GB with distal metastasis was previously reported with excellent molecular detail. 37 The case reports a primary frontotemporal GS resected and followed with TMZ/radiotherapy before the development of four ipsilateral masses 18 months later. These masses included a local recurrence, an adjacent temporal cystic mass, a cerebellar mass without connection to ventricular seeding or leptomeninges, and a concomitant solid pulmonary nodule. Histological confirmation of these recurrent tumors revealed the local recurrence as ependymomatous GB, the temporal mass as epithelioid GB, the cerebellar mass as typical gliomatous GB, and the lung biopsy as a GB metastasis. 37 The authors also reported mutation acquisition differentiating each of the subclones from their ancestral GS. While this report is informative, multicentricity in our case does not definitively explain why the distant recurrence in the left convexity does not display definitive histological characteristics of a GB or GS.

In SVZ spread, neural stem cells in the SVZ act as reservoirs of early mutation-harboring progenitors that drive recurrence independently of the primary tumor through cyclic and repetitive evolution. [38][39][40] Primary and recurrent tumors may or may not share direct clonal linkage between each other except for the shared mutations involved in the SVZ. This suggests that recurrence may reflect evolution from a shared early progenitor clone in the SVZ, rather than directly originating from a dominant or treatment-resistant primary tumor clone. 38 The implication of this finding for this case is that the primary and recurrent tumors may instead reflect two distinct distal tumors generated through SVZ cyclic evolution, with the second tumor acquiring a new TP53 mutation and taking on a predominantly sarcomatous phenotype. This would mean that an underlying subset of SVZ neural stem cells with minimally preserved mutational burden uniquely migrated to two distal sites. While this would reflect an exceptional oncogenic mechanism, the probability of such a profound clonal evolution to a non-GB tumor is exceptionally low. This SVZ mechanism may describe the occurrence and recurrence of the primary tumor, but likely still fails to account for the distal sarcomatoid recurrence. This conclusion is again complicated by the lack of histological and molecular data on the local recurrence, and the lack of SVZ tissue for assessment of neural stem cell subpopulations.

Finally, little is known about the response of GSs to traditional sarcoma-directed chemotherapy. The previously reported patient with noncontiguous GS and extracranial metastases underwent a sarcoma-directed chemotherapy regimen including adriamycin and ifosfamide, but the approach was unsuccessful. 16 Treatments like bevacizumab with irinotecan, erlotinib with TMZ, and pathway inhibitors demonstrate emerging utility in the management of recurrent GB and GS. [41][42][43] However, the rarity of secondary GS, and subsequently predominantly sarcomatous distant clones, is an extreme limitation in developing clinical trials and novel treatment regimens for such patients. At this time, it is difficult to predict whether such a sarcomatoid tumor would respond to classical sarcoma therapies, or whether standard GS resection with chemoradiotherapy remains superior.

div.head: Lessons
div.p: This case contributes to the evolving understanding of GS as both a primary and treatment-emergent phenotype. The predominance of sarcomatoid morphology, alongside an acquired TP53 mutation, may illustrate how GB could evolve under therapeutic selective pressure into a more aggressive, mesenchymal differentiated clone with the capacity for noncontiguous dissemination, while still preserving the underlying molecular signature of the tumor of origin. A key strength of this case is the detailed histopathological and molecular characterization of both primary and secondary lesions, enabling inference of clonal evolution and mutational progression. Limitations include the absence of SNP microarray data for the distal recurrent tumor due to insufficient DNA quality and the lack of tissue-based confirmation of the histological, immunohistochemical, and molecular phenotype of the local recurrence, which constrains conclusions about the anatomical and temporal sequence of transformation. Consequently, the sequence of molecular evolution or potential for multiclonal origin remains uncertain for this case. While this uncertainty could represent a relevant retroactive justification for biopsying the locally recurrent tumor, this was not in keeping with the goals of care for this patient.

Clinically, this case reinforces the importance of tissue confirmation in atypical recurrences. It highlights the limitations of imaging alone in assessing disease progression and the diagnostic value of rebiopsy in guiding appropriate management, particularly as secondary GS (especially with TP53 mutation) is associated with poor prognosis. 21 Treatment and diagnostic pathways of distally recurrent tumors may need to prioritize rebiopsy of prior lesion sites or, alternatively, include further subclonal characterization of primary tumors to inform the potential for resistant subpopulations or clonal evolution. By more accurately characterizing the clonal origins and evolutionary drivers of GB, research may be able to identify more specific targets for treatment and intervention.

In this case, the patient remained clinically and radiographically stable for 11 months following initial resection. However, upon radiographic identification of a noncontiguous recurrence, the patient experienced rapid neurological decline, including complete right lower extremity paralysis within 3 weeks. Following interim histopathological identification of a high-grade sarcomatoid tumor with some focal glioma-like immunophenotypic features, the patient elected to forgo further treatment and died 2 weeks later. This case exemplifies how clonal evolution under therapy-induced selective pressure may drive atypical, extra-axial, or anatomically discordant recurrences. It reinforces the necessity of tissue diagnosis in such cases to align clinical decision-making, and provides a rare illustration of the aggressive nature of noncontiguous clonally evolved GB recurrence.

figure.figDesc: FIG. 1. Postcontrast T1-weighted MR images. A: Coronal image obtained in February 2023 showing right temporal ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis and vasogenic edema (arrow), consistent with GB. B: Coronal image obtained in May 2023 showing radiotherapy isodose field delivering 60 Gy in 30 fractions. C: Coronal image obtained in June 2023 showing right temporal resection cavity with an enhancing border (arrow). D: Coronal image obtained in January 2024 showing small, enhancing lesion along the inferior margin of the right temporal resection cavity (arrow), suggestive of local recurrence. E: Coronal image obtained in February 2023 showing normal left convexity anatomy with no radiographic evidence of disease. F: Axial image obtained in May 2023 showing radiotherapy isodose field delivering 60 Gy in 30 fractions. G: Coronal image obtained in June 2023 showing normal left convexity anatomy with no radiographic evidence of disease. H: Coronal image obtained in January 2024 showing separate enhancing extra-axial mass at the left parasagittal convexity (red arrow) with dural thickening and bone involvement (white arrow).

figure.head: FIG. 2 .
figure.figDesc: FIG. 2. Pathological findings of primary GB. A: Hematoxylin-phloxine-saffron staining showing pleomorphic glial neoplasm with microvascular proliferation. B: Staining immunopositive for GFAP. C: Staining immunonegative for IDH1 R132H. D: Staining showing retained ATRX nuclear expression. E: Staining approximately 40% nuclei immunopositive for p53. F: Staining ≥ 20% immunopositive for Ki-67. Original magnification for all panels ×40.

figure.head: FIG. 3 .
figure.figDesc: FIG. 3. Pathological findings of noncontiguous sarcomatoid tumor. A: Hematoxylin-phloxine-saffron staining showing pleomorphic spindle-shaped tumor cells within a dense collagen matrix. B: Hematoxylin-phloxine-saffron staining showing extracranial margin. C: Hematoxylin-phloxinesaffron staining showing extracranial margin. D: Staining showing extracranial margin with focus of GFAP-positive tumor cells within dense collagen matrix. E: Reticulin silver staining highlighting connective tissue matrix. F and G: Stainings of tumor diffusely immunopositive for vimentin (cytoplasmic) (F) and p53 (nuclear) (G). H: Staining approximately 15%-20% immunopositive for Ki-67. Original magnification ×40 (A, C, F, and G), ×5 (B), ×10 (D), and ×20 (E and H).
